Diverting loop ileostomy/colonic lavage An alternative surgical intervention that has been associated low mortality in some studies. 43 Additional Therapies Leukocytapheresis (LCAP) is useful in the management of TM. A series of six patients whose conditions had failed to improve after treatment with high-dose steroids and antibiotics were enrolled in a study. In four cases, the TM resolved by the morning after initiation of treatment with LCAP. In two patients, the TM resolved approximately 40 hours later. Improvement continued in four out of the six patients. 44

Shetler et al reported that colonoscopic decompression and intracolonic vancomycin administration in the management of acute pseudomembranous colitis associated with TM is safe and effective in approximately 57–71% of the cases. 45 Hyperbaric oxygen therapy has also been reported to be effective in the management of TM, but further studies are needed to confirm these results. 46 Tacrolimus was successfully used in 1 case study in a patient with steroid-refractory UC complicated by TM. However, further studies are required to validate its use. 47

Intravenous immune globulin (IVIG) may potentially be an adjunct therapy in patients with severe C diff infection with megacolon, taking into account the possibility of adverse effects. 48 Special Populations HIV/AIDS patients An aggressive exploration of infectious and noninfectious etiology is a must, including radiological imaging and early limited endoscopic workup. Patients with cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis or C. diff infection respond poorly to medical management only and often require surgical intervention. 49 , 50 Critically ill patients with advanced AIDS who are poor surgical candidates could be managed by supportive therapy, antibiotics, and careful colonic decompression.

Pregnant women Women with known risk factors for TM (most commonly UC) should plan conception during a state of remission. 51 Patients who are in remission at the conception are likely to remain in remission during pregnancy. In the case of TM in pregnancy primarily due to UC, high-dose intravenous glucocorticoids therapy is effective in three-fourth cases of severe colitis, the remainder requiring either Infliximab or emergent surgical intervention. 52 , 53

Management of fulminant colitis during pregnancy is challenging as the gravid uterus can restrict a thorough abdominal examination, and diagnostic radiation could be teratogenic. 54 In pregnancy, hemoglobin, and serum albumin level drop, while other inflammatory markers, including the ESR and CRP rise; so, these blood tests are not reliable measures of disease activity. Urgent colon surgery can increase the risks of preterm delivery and spontaneous abortions.

Prognosis The mortality rates for TM are inconsistent. Before 1976, the death rate in 604 cases of TM was 27 percent (43 out of 160) for patients who were managed medically and 19 percent in 444 patients who underwent surgical intervention. 55 The in-hospital mortality for TM further decreased from 9.2 to 6.5 percent in 2010 through 2014. 4 Colonic perforation is associated with a significantly worse prognosis, with the mortality rate increased by three- to fivefold. 6 , 8

The etiology of TM can also affect the prognosis, TM secondary to infectious etiology has a better prognosis than patients with TM secondary to IBD who have been treated with biologics; however, this result is mainly based upon a small group of studies. The prognosis is especially good when colonic dilatation complicates acute self-limited colitis and is managed promptly. 56 Nevertheless, the mortality rates dropped significantly to less than 2 percent in patients with IBD, probably related to diverse factors, including early identification of TM, the rapid escalation from glucocorticoid therapy to biologics (or cyclosporine), increasing use of biologics and accelerated dosing, aggressive medical management, prompt surgical intervention, and better post-surgical care. 9

A review of patients with TM due to C. diff infection between 1968 and 1992 revealed an overall mortality of 31 to 35 percent. 31 In other studies, the overall mortality from TM secondary to severe C. diff infection was 64 to 67 percent, and 71 to 100 percent in cases which were managed surgically. 31 , 57 These studies show that patients with TM due to C. diff infection will do better with medical management alone, and surgery may offer a nominal benefit. However, surgery should not be postponed in acutely sick patients.

The difference in mortality rates may also be due to the biases of medical or surgical providers. Two studies have revealed that 68 to 75 percent of cases of TM managed medically did not require a surgical intervention later and have maintained remission for up to six years. 6 , 9 Surgical studies reveal up to a 50 percent rate of future surgical intervention, including colectomy in patients with TM who initially responded well to medical treatment alone. 55 , 58 Timely surgical interventions decreased the mortality rate significantly from 22 to 1.2 percent in one report. 59 The key points of this review article have been summarized in Table 3 . Table 3 Key Points to Keep in Mind when managing Toxic Megacolon

Key points of the Review Article: 1. Toxic megacolon (TM) was thought to be a complication for ulcerative colitis (UC) specifically. Later on, the Crohn’s disease (CD) was found to be a cause, and gradually it becomes evident that any inflammatory condition of the colon could predispose to TM. 2. Accurate history and physical examination, plain radiographs of the abdomen, sigmoidoscopy and, most important of all, awareness of the condition facilitate diagnosis in most cases. 3. The most common cause of hospital admission included Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) (51.6%), followed by septicemia (10.2%) and intestinal infections (4.1%).

4. Computed tomography of the abdomen with contrast is usually performed to establish the diagnosis and also evaluating for complications that may require immediate surgery. Baseline and serial abdominal x rays are then performed to follow the progression of colonic dilatation. 5. Patients should be admitted and evaluated, preferably in the intensive care unit, with frequent examinations to assess for signs of toxicity. 6. Both medical and surgical teams should co-manage patients on admission with daily evaluation.

7. Female gender, age more than 40 years, hypoalbuminemia, acidosis, and high blood urea nitrogen levels are associated with high mortality in a previous study. This patient population requires a special attention from the admission. 8. It is important to examine the abdomen for hepatic dullness every day in patients who have severe colitis and are taking high-dose glucocorticoids because they might have a free perforation and not have classic signs of peritonitis. 9. The main goal for treatment for TM is to treat the underlying inflammation, restoring colonic motility, and preventing free colonic perforation.

10. In HIV infection patients with TM, an aggressive search for infectious and noninfectious causes is essential, including early limited endoscopy and imaging studies. Patients with cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis or C. difficile infection respond poorly to medical therapy and often require emergent subtotal colectomy and ileostomy. 11. Women with known risk factors for toxic megacolon (most commonly ulcerative colitis) should plan conception during a state of remission.

Conclusion TM is a condition best approached through the combined efforts of the medical and surgical team working with the patient. Medical therapy is the first-line treatment in most cases, but objective measures of improvement should be discussed before treatment initiation. If the patient manifests signs of hemorrhage, peritonitis, or perforation, surgery is emergently indicated. Subtotal/total colectomy and ileostomy is the procedure of choice in most instances, and a laparoscopic approach is potentially favored when possible and feasible.

Malignant ascites develops when malignant disease of the peritoneum, typically from an underlying gastrointestinal or gynecologic cancer, causes excess fluid to accumulate in the abdominal cavity. The development of malignant ascites portends a poor prognosis and is associated with debilitating symptoms and a reduced quality of life. While several palliative therapies exist for the management of these symptoms, none have proven curative or have demonstrated a prolonged therapeutic benefit. Thus, various experimental treatments are currently under investigation. These include immunotherapies and targeted therapies, monoclonal antibodies, herbal derivatives, viral therapies, devices, and more. Introduction Malignant ascites (MA) arises in the setting of malignant peritoneal disease as a manifestation of underlying gastrointestinal or gynecological cancer metastases. Peritoneal metastases are typically associated with a worse survival when compared to other metastatic sites. Furthermore, MA is an indicator of advanced disease associated with debilitating symptomatology including abdominal discomfort, nausea, vomiting, and anorexia. 1

The management of MA is challenging, particularly in cases in which surgical treatment of the underlying cancer is not feasible. In these cases, the aim of regional or surgical management is palliation. While many palliative approaches are described in the literature, the effectiveness of these treatments is often limited and temporary. In recent years, there has been growing interest in novel therapeutic approaches for the management of MA, including targeted therapies, immunotherapies, herbal derivatives, and devices. The purpose of this review is to provide a contemporary representation of these emerging therapies.

2. Current Standard Therapies Today, there are five primary treatments used in the management of MA: paracentesis, diuretics, peritoneovenous shunting, permanent catheters, and intraperitoneal (i.p.) chemotherapy. Clinician preference on their use varies widely. 2 The most commonly used treatment is serial paracenteses, which can drain several liters of i.p. fluid and palliate common symptoms in approximately 90% of patients. 2 , 3 Unfortunately, symptoms often returns within several weeks as the ascitic fluid reaccumulates, and serial paracenteses carry increasing risk of infection, bowel perforation, peritonitis, hypotension, and protein and electrolyte disturbances. 4

For those requiring serial paracenteses and who have a life expectancy of greater than 2–3 months, permanent catheters are often used. 5 The advantages include increased patient autonomy due to self-drainage, increased convenience due to fewer hospital visits, and decreased discomfort due to fewer procedures. 6 MA control can be achieved in 83% to 100% of patients with a mean patency duration exceeding 50 days, and some case reports have shown effective functionality for well over one year. 4 , 7 However, it is limited by common complications such as peritonitis, leakage, infections, catheter occlusion, and hypotension. 8

Standard medical management involves diuretic therapy, with nearly two-thirds of physicians prescribing diuretics for MA. 2 However, due to variability in regimens and few trials assessing their efficacy, there is no consensus on their role in MA, and fewer than half of prescribing physicians consider them effective. A prior review of several cohort studies and case reports, however, suggests that 40–45% of patients may derive some benefit. 1 Importantly, serum ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) > 1.1 g/dL and MA from hepatic metastases portend a more favorable response. 9 It appears that the efficacy of this therapy is largely dependent upon the biology underlying the development of MA.

Peritoneovenous shunting uses a one-way valve to return ascitic fluid to the venous system. 10 It allows for fewer paracenteses and preserves serum albumin levels, but has an inferior control rate compared to paracentesis and a mean patency of as little as 9 weeks. 1 It also requires perioperative hospitalization, is associated with several risks including shunt occlusion, ascitic leak, coagulopathy, infection, bleeding, and even death, and is contraindicated in several conditions such as heart failure and renal failure. 1 , 4 , 11 For these reasons, it is typically reserved for patients who have failed other modalities.

Finally, i.p. chemotherapy, typically used in conjunction with cytoreductive surgery (CRS) to treat peritoneal carcinomatosis, has shown some benefit in MA even when an optimal cytoreduction is not possible. The hypothesized mechanism is the targeting of microscopic tumor cells on the peritoneal surface from which MA is produced and the inducement of a fibrotic reaction that prevents the reformation of fluid. Pharmacokinetic evidence also suggests that compared to systemic chemotherapy, i.p. treatments improve drug concentrations within the peritoneum, allow for prolonged therapeutic effects, limit systemic toxicities, and more directly target malignant cells. 12 However, these effects depend upon the specific chemotherapy regimen chosen. While some, such as mitoxantrone and mustard agents, have fallen out of favor, other agents such as bleomycin, taxanes, and platinum-based agents have been shown to improve symptoms in up to two-thirds of patients. 1 , 13 – 15 Hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) has been widely adopted due to evidence that superheating the chemotherapy to at least 40 degrees Celsius increases cytotoxicity to improve tissue penetration and selectively targets malignant cells within the peritoneal cavity. 16

3. Novel Therapies While these therapies provide palliative benefits in the management of MA, each is limited by side effects and lack of a prolonged therapeutic benefit. As a result, various experimental therapies are under investigation in the hopes of finding a novel solution to this condition. 3.1 Immunotherapy and Targeted Therapy Immunotherapies and targeted therapies have gained interest in the past decade in the management of both solid tumors and MA. 17 While most studies on the subject are small and inconclusive, several therapies have shown preliminary efficacy.

3.1.1 VEGF Inhibitors It is thought that one of the causes of MA is the obstruction of draining lymphatics by tumor cells. 18 In the 1980’s investigators speculated that the underlying culprit in this phenomenon is the secretion of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) by tumor cells, given that VEGF is more concentrated in MA compared to non-malignant ascites and more prevalent in metastatic as compared to localized tumors. 19 , 20 As such, VEGF inhibition became a target in the treatment of MA ( Table 1a ).

Early case series showed that the VEGF inhibitor bevacizumab, administered both i.p. and orally, produced symptomatic relief and a reduction in the ascites reaccumulation rate in several women with refractory MA from ovarian cancer. 21 – 26 Two clinical trials were subsequently initiated. In 2012, researchers randomized 55 patients with recurrent MA from ovarian cancer to receive either placebo or i.v. aflibercept, a recombination human protein and a VEGF inhibitor, every 2 weeks. 27 Although the aflibercept group experienced better mean time to paracentesis (TTP) (55.1 days versus 23.3 days) and paracentesis-free survival (PFS) (42.0 days versus 18.0 days), there was no difference in overall survival (OS). Furthermore, 3 patients in the aflibercept group developed intestinal perforations that led to death, as compared to just 1 patient in the placebo group that developed an intestinal fistula that led to fatal sepsis. Gastrointestinal complications such as perforation are well-known side effects of VEGF inhibitors and their use in this patient population should be undertaken with caution. 28 A smaller single-arm study investigating i.v. aflibercept in a similar patient population found that 10 of 16 patients achieved a 2-fold increase in TTP. 29 Unfortunately, one patient suffered an intestinal perforation.

Randomized trials have also been conducted with VEGF inhibitors administered intraperitoneally. In 2016, researchers randomized 53 patients with advanced gastrointestinal cancers and MA to i.p. bevacizumab or placebo. 30 Median PFS was greater in the bevacizumab group compared to the placebo group, though to a non-statistically significant degree. There were no major gastrointestinal events. In 2021 a phase II trial found that in 24 women with MA from ovarian cancer, treatment with i.p. bevacizumab resulted in a 4.3-fold increase in median PFS, though 1 patient developed a perforation and 3 developed a bowel obstruction. 31 A dose-escalation study of i.p. bevacizumab in 13 patients with refractory MA found a disease control rate of 61.5%, with a grade 3 bowel obstruction serving as the dose-limiting toxicity. 32

Although VEGF inhibitors carry safety concerns around gastrointestinal perforation and obstruction, these studies demonstrate promising improvements in refractory MA that should be weighed against these risks. 3.1.2 Interferons Interferons (IFN) alpha and gamma are signaling cytokines used to treat a variety of infectious, autoimmune, and inflammatory conditions. They exert their effects through both direct cytotoxicity and immune cell stimulation. Interferons have been evaluated in the management of various cancers, though their use specifically in MA remains limited with few full-text studies available for review ( Table 1b ).

The study of IFNs to treat MA arose in the 1980’s when clinicians incidentally found improvement of ascites in patients with refractory ovarian cancer who were administered IFNs as salvage therapy. For example, researchers administered human leukocyte IFN intramuscularly to 5 patients with advanced ovarian carcinoma and found that both patients with pre-treatment MA showed a significant reduction in their ascites production. 33 Similarly, i.p. cisplatin and IFN alpha administered to 24 patients with advanced ovarian cancer resulted in resolution of ascites for 3–7 months in the 3 patients with pre-treatment ascites. 34

Following these trials, IFNs were studied as a stand-alone treatment in MA, with mixed results. Ten patients with MA from ovarian cancer were treated with i.p. IFN alpha-2b every 2 weeks for 1–4 treatments, but just half reported symptomatic improvement in abdominal distension and girth. 35 Five of 13 (38%) patients with MA from ovarian cancer responded to treatment with i.p. IFN alpha-2b, though all 5 responders had MA only without masses. 36 Similarly, there was a 40% response rate in 14 patients with MA refractory to chemotherapy treated with i.p. IFN beta, though it’s unclear how the authors defined response rate. 37 Finally, a pilot study of 41 patients with MA again showed moderately positive results. 38 After six 6-hour infusions of i.p. IFN alpha-2b, 12 patients had a complete response, 15 had a partial response, and 14 had no response; the mean time to fluid reaccumulation increased from 11.4 days pre-treatment to 70.5 days post-treatment.
Given these mixed results, the use of IFNs in the management of MA remains experimental with significant effort needed to identify appropriate dosages and treatment regimens.

3.1.3 Tumor Necrosis Factor Tumor necrosis factor (TNF) is a pro-inflammatory cytokine implicated in the formation of MA as well as being leveraged as a therapeutic, a dual effect first demonstrated in mouse models of MA from ovarian adenocarcinoma. 39 After early pharmacokinetic trials of TNF in patients with solid tumors demonstrated feasibility and safety, a trial of its use in MA was conducted in 1990. 40 In this study, 23 patients with refractory MA from ovarian cancer were treated with i.p. human recombinant TNF ( Table 1c ). 41 While 20 patients experienced a reduction in ascites for at least 4 weeks, the full text is not available and further details are lacking. A phase I trial published in 1991 produced similarly positive results. 42 In 29 patients with refractory MA from various primary cancers, i.p. TNF-alpha once weekly for between 0–2 months produced a complete response in 16 patients and a partial response in 6 patients.

However, a trial in 39 patients with symptomatic MA from ovarian carcinoma or primary peritoneal carcinoma randomized to either paracentesis or paracentesis plus i.p. TNF-alpha was discouraging. 43 No patients in either arm had a complete or partial response, and adverse events were significantly more common in the treatment group. Similarly, 302 patients with MA treated with i.p. TNF produced an objective response rate of just 46%, though the full text is not available. 44

These inconsistent results, along with the lack of full-text studies in English, present a challenge for future study, and the possibility that certain dosages of TNF may promote tumor formation makes future investigations especially difficult. 45 A single-center exploratory trial is currently underway in China investigating HIPEC with Cisplatin and i.p. recombinant human TNF in the management of MA from gynecologic cancers. 46

3.1.4 OK-432 OK-432 (Picibanil) is a freeze-dried powder developed through heating Streptococcal Pyogenes in the presence of Penicillin to eliminate the bacteria’s toxin production. 47 In the 1970’s and 1980’s, OK-432 was found to have sclerosing and anti-neoplastic activity through stimulation of natural killer cells, macrophages, neutrophils, and IFNs. 48 Given this purported anti-neoplastic, sclerosing, and immuno-stimulatory activity, in the 1980’s it gained interest in the possible palliation of MA, particularly in Eastern countries ( Table 1d ).

A 1983 abstract describes 134 patients with MA from various gastrointestinal primary tumors who were administered i.p. OK-432. 49 Ascites resolved in 76 patients and was reduced in 8 others. The treatment was more effective in patients with positive cytology, with 81.7% of these patients showing a response to therapy compared to just 24.1% of patients with negative cytology. The authors conducted a smaller study of i.p. OK-432 in 12 patients with MA from gastric cancer and found that all patients had resolution of their ascites, though likewise the full text is unavailable. 50

Toge et al. showed similarly promising results in their study of i.p. OK-432, administered either continuously or intermittently, in 25 patients with MA from various primary tumors. 51 In the continuous administration group, cytology changed from positive to negative in 100% of patients; in the intermittent group, 100% of patients who received 5 or more doses saw a change in cytology, compared to just 25% of those who received fewer than 5 doses.

Othe investigators studied different regimens of OK-432. I.p. OK-432 with Interleukin-2 was administered in patients with MA from gastric or colorectal cancer in two separate studies. 52 , 53 The response rate ranged from 81% to 100% with Interleukin-2 seemingly conferring a synergistic benefit. Other researchers randomized 41 patients with malignant effusions (31 with MA, 8 with malignant pleural effusion, and 2 with both) to receive 1 of 3 intracavitary regimens: chemotherapy alone, OK-432 alone, or combination immunochemotherapy. 54 Compared to the chemotherapy alone group, patients who received OK-432 alone or combination immunochemotherapy had greater reductions in effusion size and greater disappearance of tumor cells within MA. Furthermore, the 1-year survival rate was 0%, 0%, and 17% in the chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and combination groups, respectively. The authors concluded that intracavitary OK-432 was superior to intracavitary chemotherapy in the management of malignant effusions, but that the combination was most beneficial. The largest study to date was conducted in 1998 by reviewing 400 cases of MA from gastrointestinal malignancies treated with i.p. OK-432 over 20 years. 55 The researchers found a response rate of 60% and a reduction of tumor volume in 20% of cases, although the full text is unavailable for review.

Given this favorable response rate across hundreds of patients, the synergistic benefits when used alongside other treatments, and the suggestion that it may even improve survival in some patients, OK-432 offers a promising potential therapy that warrants investigation in the United States. 56

3.1.5 Autologous Dendritic and Natural Killer Cell Immunotherapy Autologous dendritic cell immunotherapy is an investigational immunotherapy developed by extracting cells from a patient, processing and expanding them ex vivo, and then reintroducing them. 57 Though a relatively nascent treatment modality that has mostly been studied as an anti-cancer therapy, recent case reports and studies have described its use in MA ( Table 1e ).

A 2008 case report describes a 55-year-old man whose MA secondary to metastatic lung cancer was significantly improved with cell-free and concentrated ascites re-infusion therapy alongside i.p. injections of autologous natural killer and dendritic cells taken from his tumor-draining lymph nodes. 58 A 2014 abstract describes a response rate of 40.9% and disease control rate of 77.3% in 22 patients with MA who were treated with i.p. dendritic cell vaccines with cytokine-induced killer cells. 59 Similarly, in 21 patients with MA from various cancers who underwent autologous immunotherapy with the extraction, expansion, and i.p. reinfusion of dendritic cells and natural killer cells, 8 achieved a complete or partial response, 4 experienced stable disease, and 9 developed progressive disease. 60 Some researchers have used other types of immune cells in this treatment modality, and Vc9Vd2 T cells, a specific form of T cell known to play a role in tumor and microbial defense, showed some preliminary efficacy in a small group of patients with MA from gastric cancer. 61

Though autologous i.p. immunotherapy remains exploratory, it is likely to garner interest in the future given the increasing role of immunotherapy in cancer care. Further studies of its use in MA must be conducted before recommending its routine use.

3.2 Monoclonal Antibodies Since the first production of a monoclonal antibody in 1975, these man-made proteins have gained attention for their promise to treat a variety of diseases. The role of monoclonal antibodies in MA stems from studies conducted in the 1980’s showing that ovarian cancer cells could be detected through labeling monoclonal antibodies with radioisotopes and performing immunoscintigraphy. 62 While this ultimately never reached the specificity required for these antibodies to become curative cancer treatments, their i.p. administration did localize to cancer cells within MA fairly well. 63 On the basis of these findings, investigations into their role in MA were initiated ( Table 2 ).

3.2.1 AUA1, HMFG1, HMFG2, and H17E2 The first study to assess monoclonal antibodies in MA was a case series published in 1987, in which 24 patients with MA from ovarian cancer were treated with different i.p. injections of 131 I-labeled monoclonal antibodies commonly expressed in ovarian, breast, and gastrointestinal adenocarcinomas: HMFG1, HMFG2, AUA1, and H17E2. 64 Of the 5 patients with MA upon presentation, just 1 demonstrated control of MA for 6 months, though the authors noted that all 5 patients had large-volume disease.

In 1988 researchers studied the use of i.p. AUA1 and HMFG2 in two groups: patients with refractory ovarian cancer without ascites and patients with MA refractory to paracentesis and diuretics. 65 None of the 7 patients with ovarian carcinoma saw meaningful tumor regression after treatment with 131 I-conjugated HMFG2. However, in the 5 patients with recurrent MA treated with either the 131 I-conjugated HMFG2 or AUA1 antibody, 3 experienced ascites resolution for a mean of 4 months, 1 died early but had seen disappearance of tumor cells in his ascitic fluid, and 1 experienced progression but had a subpopulation of tumor cells that were antigen-negative. Though these results were not conclusive, they nonetheless demonstrated an early proof-of-concept.

3.2.3 Catumaxomab Trifunctional antibodies have binding sites for 3 different antigens or receptors: CD3 on T-cells, a specific tumor antigen, and the Fc-y receptor on accessory immune cells. 66 This trifunctionality allows these antibodies to exert their anti-neoplastic effects through several pathways, potentially making them superior to bispecific antibodies.

In early preclinical studies, Catumaxomab was shown to be particularly promising. A mouse/rat monoclonal antibody, it binds to CD3 on T-cells, the Fc-y receptor on accessory immune cells, and the EpCAM antigen, which is found in 70% to 100% of the tumor cells in malignant effusions and is considered a tumor-specific antigen in MA. 67 Clinical trials of Catumaxomab in MA were initiated in the early 2000’s, and in 2009 it was approved for use in the European Union.

In 2005 investigators studied both Catumaxomab and Rexomun, a trifunctional antibody that targets Her2/neu, in 8 patients with symptomatic MA from peritoneal carcinomatosis. 68 Four received Catumaxomab, 1 received Rexomun, and 3 received both; all trifunctional antibodies were administered i.p. over 6–8 hours. All patients experienced relief of symptoms and a reduction in ascites, which correlated with significant drops in the proportion of EpCAM- and HER2/neu-positive tumor cells in the MA. Nearly all patients experienced flu-like symptoms, though none were forced to discontinue treatment.

These investigators then conducted a trial of paracentesis with or without Catumaxomab in 258 patients with MA, stratified by ovarian versus non-ovarian origin. 69 Patients underwent four 6-hour i.p. Catutaxomab infusions. In both the ovarian and non-ovarian groups, the Catumaxomab group had a better PFS (46 days versus 11 days) and median TTP (77 days vs 13 days). Furthermore, OS was significantly prolonged in the subset of patients with gastric cancer. Nearly 90% of patients received all 4 doses and side effects were tolerable. Similarly, in 23 patients with MA from ovarian cancer, four 6-hour infusions of i.p. Catumaxomab produced a 99.9% mean reduction in the number of EpCAM-positive tumor cells within ascites and resulted in 22 of 23 patients not requiring paracentesis between the first and last days of the study (a total of 37 days). 70 A 2007 abstract

Further trials investigated whether Catumaxomab could be administered as a 3-hour infusion as opposed to a 6-hour infusion, which would allow it to be given on an outpatient basis. While these studies showed positive results, the prevalence of adverse events, including nausea, vomiting, pyrexia, and abdominal pain, limited its feasibility as an outpatient treatment. 71 , 72 In one trial, 40% of patients had to postpone or discontinue treatments due to adverse events despite improvements in TTP and PFS, and the CASIMAS trial showed that nearly half of patients randomized to 3-hour i.p. infusions of Catumaxomab with or without prednisone experienced grade 3 or greater adverse events, with prednisone conferring little benefit on the side effect profile. 73 , 74 Furthermore, it was found that i.p. Catumaxomab may be less feasible in patients undergoing surgery for their disease. For example, researchers treated 41 patients with ovarian cancer undergoing CRS and systemic chemotherapy for their disease with i.p. Catumaxomab administered as an intraoperative bolus followed by 3-hour infusions given on postoperative days 7, 10, 13, and 16. 75 Just 61% of patients completed all 5 postoperative infusions, 95% experienced a Catumaxomab-associated adverse event, and 51% experienced postoperative complications that prevented further Catumaxomab treatments in 22% of patients. While Catumaxomab was not necessarily implicated in these postoperative complications, the authors speculated that the cytokine release associated with its use may have contributed to an inflammatory environment and increased the risk of surgical complications.

Catumaxomab remains the only trifunctional monoclonal antibody approved for the treatment of MA, and several trials have proven its efficacy in palliating symptoms and prolonging PFS and TTP. Larger trials are underway investigating its use across different settings, including intra-operatively, alongside systemic chemotherapy, and as a stand-alone therapy for refractory MA. Nevertheless, its side effects can sometimes be prohibitive and it may not be appropriate in the tenuous postoperative setting.

3.2.4 Other monoclonal antibodies Several other monoclonal antibodies have been investigated in the management of MA. HEA125xOKT3, which is directed against the EpCAM antigen and the CD3 antigen found on T lymphocytes, resulted in a complete response in 8 patients and a partial response in 2 patients when injected i.p. in 10 patients suffering from MA from refractory ovarian carcinoma. 76 I.p. nivolumab produced symptomatic improvement and no further need for paracentesis in a 71-year-old patient with pancreatic cancer and MA refractory to conventional treatments. 77 2G3, an anti-mucin antibody with known reactivity against effusions from breast and ovarian tumors, demonstrated mixed results as an 131 I-radioloabeled i.p. injection in patients with MA from ovarian or breast cancer, with just 4 of 9 patients experiencing resolution or control of ascites. 78 While several other small studies have been conducted on the use of monoclonal antibodies in MA, the results have been largely inconclusive and none have demonstrated results comparable to those seen with Catumaxomab. 79

3.3 Endostar Endostar is a modified recombinant form of endostatin, a collagen fragment that has been shown to inhibit VEGF-induced tumor angiogenesis and proliferation. 80 It was approved in China in 2005 for the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer and has shown good results in the treatment of MPE, though its investigation in MA is somewhat limited. 81

Most studies assessing Endostar in MA have randomized patients to receive either i.p. Endostar plus i.p. platinum-based chemotherapy or i.p. platinum-based chemotherapy alone. A 2015 meta-analysis of 25 of these randomized trials encompassing 1,253 patients with malignant serious effusions showed that the i.p. Endostar group had a significantly better effusion response rate (76% versus 48%) and improvement rate in quality of life (69% versus 44%) compared to the i.p. chemotherapy alone group. 82 However, most of these studies were conducted in patients with MPEs only as opposed to MA, which are typically more responsive to intracavitary treatments.

A more recent study in 90 patients with MA from gastric cancer showed that patients who received i.p. Endostar in addition to I.p. cisplatin had a better OS, response rate, disease control rate, and improvement rate in quality of life compared to patients who received i.p. cisplatin alone, without a major difference in the rate of ascites response. 83 While these results are promising, we lack robust randomized trials conducted in the U.S. demonstrating a definitive benefit to Endostar in MA.

3.4 Steroids Some researchers have reasoned that steroids could play a role in MA, as they have been shown to downregulate VEGF and have proven effective as i.p. injections in patients with refractory ascites from end-stage renal disease. 84 With this in mind, researchers treated 15 patients with recurrent MA with i.p. Triamcinolone Hexacetonide. 85 While 13 of 15 patients required repeat paracenteses, the interval between paracenteses increased from 9.5 days to 17.5 days and self-assessed symptoms improved. Interestingly, all 7 patients whose paracentesis interval doubled after the treatment had a narrow SAAG (< 11 g/L). Because a narrow SAAG is often caused by abnormal increases in capillary permeability and is associated with elevated VEGF expression, the authors speculated that the i.p. steroid treatment functioned through inhibition of VEGF expression. A case report was also published of a man with MA from non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma whose paracentesis interval increased from 2 weeks to 8 weeks following treatment with i.p. triamcinolone acetonide. 86 Although these appear to be the only studies investigating i.p. steroids in MA, perhaps further investigation will be conducted in the future.

3.5 Oncolytic Viral Therapy Oncolytic viruses are experimental cancer treatments that function through direct tumor cell lysis and activation of an immune response. They have been studied in solid organ tumors but their investigation in MA is confined to just a handful of studies. 87 However, it is biologically plausible that oncolytic viral therapy may be more effective in MA compared to solid tumors, as MA is easier to penetrate due to the relatively less dense and less hypoxic microenvironment. 88

Following preclinical mouse studies showing that i.p. injections of oncolytic viruses inhibited MA, a human study was conducted in 2022 in which 40 patients with MA from various GI cancers were administered i.p. human type 5 recombinant adenovirus (H101), an oncolytic virus genetically modified to selectively replicate only in cells with mutated p53 genes. 89 The ascites response rate was 40% and the ascites control rate was 75%, and immunocytology showed tumor cell depletion and increased dendritic cells and CD8+ T cells. Side effects were tolerable. Though these results are somewhat positive and oncolytic viral therapy has garnered significant interest in cancer treatment more broadly, few conclusions can be drawn about its use in MA at this time.

3.6 Cell-free and Concentrated Ascites Reinfusion Therapy Cell-free and concentrated ascites reinfusion therapy (CART) is a novel treatment for MA that has only been tested in Japan. The process involves draining ascites, filtering out its cellular components while leaving behind proteins such as albumin, concentrating it to decrease total volume, and finally reinfusing it intravenously. The theoretical benefit of this procedure is the avoidance of protein depletion that can occur with paracentesis.

To date, there is no randomized control trial comparing CART to paracentesis. However, a systematic review following a meta-analysis of CART therapy for MA was published in 2021 and included 15 papers encompassing a total 2567 patients and 6013 procedures. 90 On average, 4.29 L of MA was collected and 0.49 L was reinfused; mean body weight fell by 3.38 kg and abdominal circumference fell by 7.86 cm; serum albumin increased by 0.14 mg/dL. Symptoms such as abdominal distension, dyspnea, and fatigue improved in most patients, and some studies reported improvements in performance status. The mean TTP following treatment was 20.7 days. Thus, while CART was developed to negate the protein depletion seen with paracentesis, it may have symptomatic benefits as well. Although this treatment modality has yet to gain traction in the U.S., it continues to be tested in Japan.

3.7 Compound Kushen Injection Compound Kushen injection (CKI) is a traditional Chinese medicine formula derived from two Chinese herbs, Kushen and Baituling. 91 It has been approved by China’s National Medical Product Administration as a treatment for cancer since 1995 and has recently been investigated in the treatment of MA. Proposed mechanisms of action include promotion of apoptosis, inhibition of angiogenesis, and suppression of the cell cycle and DNA repair pathways.

A systematic review and meta-analysis published in 2023 evaluated all trials comparing i.p chemotherapy with or without CKI in the management of MA. 91 In 17 studies encompassing 1,200 patients, the objective response rate was significantly improved in patients receiving i.p. CKI plus chemotherapy compared to i.p. chemotherapy alone (80.8% vs 61.7%). Despite these results, the authors noted that many of the included studies were small, had heterogenous populations, did not follow patients for extended periods of time, and had highly variable regimens of chemotherapy and CKI. The authors warned that larger randomized trials must be conducted before recommending the product in MA.

Like many of the experimental regimens previously described, CKI has garnered significant interest in various Asian countries but has yet to be thoroughly tested in the U.S. As a result, generalizing the results remains challenging, and it should be considered an interesting novel treatment that still requires much more research.

3.8 Octreotide Octreotide is a synthetic medication that mimics the hormone somatostatin and is used in several conditions including bleeding varices, hormone-producing tumors, and diseases of gastrointestinal hypersecretion. Known to inhibit VEGF, its use in MA was first described in case reports published in the 1990’s that showed modest palliative relief in some patients with symptomatic MA who received systemic Octreotide. 92 , 93 Researchers followed these case reports with a pilot study of 33 patients with symptomatic MA who were randomized to receive either intramuscular octreotide or intramuscular sodium chloride. 94 The octreotide group had a longer median TTP (28 days versus 14 days), though this was lost after adjusting for abdominal girth and volume of extracted fluid. Similarly, although the octreotide group reported significantly improved abdominal bloating, abdominal discomfort, and shortness of breath relative to the control group, overall quality of life was not significantly different. Based on these findings, the authors were unable to conclude whether octreotide provided a palliative benefit. A clinical trial is currently underway to further study octreotide in MA. 95

3.9 Automated Pump Device The alfapump device is a low-flow automated pump device produced in Switzerland. Implanted subcutaneously and battery-powered, the pump is connected to both the peritoneal cavity and the bladder through catheters, allowing for steady excretion of ascites through urination. 96

First tested in small groups of patients with non-malignant ascites, in 2018 researchers described the use of the alfapump in MA. 97 In the case report, a woman with recurrent MA from breast cancer underwent alfapump implantation under general anesthesia. Her daily ascites pump volume was set at 800mL per day and she did not require further paracentesis during a 14-month follow-up. Unfortunately, there is no further discussion of complications from the pump, or whether other interventions were required. In 2019, a study was published describing the alfapump in 17 patients with MA from various primary tumors. 98 Median pump survival was 89 days, with the pump in-situ in 16 of 17 patients at the time of death or the end of the study period. Furthermore, the median number of paracenteses in a 30-day period decreased from 1.3 pre-implant to 0.08 post-implant. Unfortunately, 12 adverse events occurred in 5 patients, 7 of which were pump-related and included infection, peritonitis, wound dehiscence, and renal failure. Four other patients experienced technical issues with the pump, including pump occlusion, catheter occlusion, and pump failure due to humidity.

Although the alfapump offer several benefits to ascites management, including the ability to set a “low-flow” rate that allows for continuous drainage and avoids the electrolyte and hemodynamic disturbances seen in paracentesis, it has a high rate of complications. Furthermore, patient must be maintained on long-term antibiotic prophylaxis, recharging the battery requires transcutaneous induction twice per day, and the procedure itself requires an extended hospital stay. 96 Nonetheless, it is a novel treatment for MA that perhaps will be improved upon in the coming years.

4. Mucinous Ascites Mucinous ascites is a defining feature of pseudomyxoma peritonei, a rare syndrome characterized by the diffuse accumulation of mucin-producing cancer cells within the peritoneum. Because the accumulated mucin in pseudomyxoma peritonei is characteristically gelatinous and viscous, it is particularly difficult to treat and is often refractory to many of the methods used in non-mucinous MA. Nonetheless, several “mucolytic” therapies have been investigated.

A combination of bromelain and acetylcysteine (BromAc) has been described for the treatment of mucinous ascites. Bromelain is a proteinase extract from pineapple used as a digestive aid and as an analgesic and anti-inflammatory, while acetylcysteine is used to thin mucin in airway conditions. In 2021 the first phase I clinical trial was conducted in which 20 patients with mucinous tumors were treated with intratumoral or i.p. BromAc. 99 The researchers found that 73.2% of sites and 85% of patients had an objective response following a mean of 4.2 doses. Although 85% of patients experienced a total of 88 adverse events, just 11 of these were considered serious.

A combination of celecoxib and myrtol standardized has also been investigated in pseudomyxoma peritonei. Celecoxib is a selective cyclooxygenase (COX)-2 inhibitor used in joint pain and arthritis but with potential apoptotic activity in colorectal adenomas, while myrtol standardized is an herbal product with mucolytic and anti-inflammatory properties used in airway infections. In 2022 our group described the use of this combination therapy taken orally in 13 patients with peritoneal spread from appendiceal mucinous neoplasms. 100 Although there was insufficient evidence to suggest a survival benefit or a decrease in the burden of mucinous ascites, most patients experienced a reduction in CEA levels in the 3 months after treatment compared to the 3 months before, and none suffered adverse events attributable from the therapy.

Several other agents have been investigated. Peritoneal irrigation with both sodium bicarbonate and dextrose at the time of surgery have been tested in case reports under the supposition that they could soften and dissolve mucin, but the benefits of this approach are unclear. Other agents under investigation include streptokinase, hydrogen peroxide, ascorbic acid, and N-acetyl cysteine.

5. Conclusion Malignant ascites is a debilitating condition that portends a poor prognosis and severely impacts quality of life. While various therapies, including diuretics, serial paracenteses, permanent catheters, peritoneovenous shunting, and i.p. chemotherapy can palliate some of the worst symptoms of MA, their effectiveness is often limited or temporary. Several novel therapies are currently being investigated in the management of MA to combat these shortfalls. While some have shown tremendous promise, there remains a dearth of high-quality data demonstrating superiority over current treatments. Continued research into these therapies, conducted with larger sample sizes across diverse populations, will hopefully provide better solutions for patients suffering from this challenging condition.

Use this guideline to guide referrals. If still uncertain about whether a referral is needed, consider contacting a specialist (see the recommendations on the diagnostic process ). Consider a review for people with any symptom associated with increased cancer risk who do not meet the criteria for referral or investigative action (see the recommendations on safety netting ). 1.1 Lung and pleural cancers Lung cancer 1.1.1 Refer people using a suspected cancer pathway referral for lung cancer if they: have chest X‑ray findings that suggest lung cancer, or are aged 40 and over with unexplained haemoptysis. [2015] 1.1.2

Offer an urgent , direct access chest X‑ray to assess for lung cancer in people aged 40 and over if they have 2 or more of the following unexplained symptoms, or if they have ever smoked and have 1 or more of the following unexplained symptoms: cough fatigue shortness of breath chest pain weight loss appetite loss. [2015] 1.1.3 Consider an urgent , direct access chest X‑ray to assess for lung cancer in people aged 40 and over with any of the following: persistent or recurrent chest infection finger clubbing supraclavicular lymphadenopathy or persistent cervical lymphadenopathy chest signs consistent with lung cancer thrombocytosis. [2015] Mesothelioma 1.1.4

Refer people using a suspected cancer pathway referral for mesothelioma if they have chest X‑ray findings that suggest mesothelioma. [2015] 1.1.5 Offer an urgent , direct access chest X‑ray to assess for mesothelioma in people aged 40 and over, if: they have 2 or more of the following unexplained symptoms, or they have 1 or more of the following unexplained symptoms and have ever smoked, or they have 1 or more of the following unexplained symptoms and have been exposed to asbestos: cough fatigue shortness of breath chest pain weight loss appetite loss. [2015] 1.1.6 Consider an urgent , direct access chest X‑ray to assess for mesothelioma in people aged 40 and over with either:

finger clubbing or chest signs compatible with pleural disease. [2015] 1.2 Upper gastrointestinal tract cancers Oesophageal cancer 1.2.1 Refer people using a suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal cancer if they: have dysphagia, or are aged 55 and over, with weight loss, and they have any of the following: upper abdominal pain reflux dyspepsia. [2015, amended 2025] 1.2.2 Consider non-urgent , direct access upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to assess for oesophageal cancer in people with haematemesis. [2015] 1.2.3 Consider non-urgent , direct access upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to assess for oesophageal cancer in people aged 55 or over with: treatment-resistant dyspepsia, or

upper abdominal pain with low haemoglobin levels, or raised platelet count with any of the following: nausea vomiting weight loss reflux dyspepsia upper abdominal pain, or nausea or vomiting with any of the following: weight loss reflux dyspepsia upper abdominal pain. [2015] Pancreatic cancer 1.2.4 Refer people using a suspected cancer pathway referral for pancreatic cancer if they are aged 40 and over and have jaundice. [2015] 1.2.5 Consider an urgent , direct access CT scan, or an urgent , direct access ultrasound scan if CT is not available, to assess for pancreatic cancer in people aged 60 and over with weight loss and any of the following: diarrhoea back pain abdominal pain nausea

vomiting constipation new‑onset diabetes. [2015] Stomach cancer 1.2.6 Consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for people with an upper abdominal mass consistent with stomach cancer. [2015] 1.2.7 Refer people using a suspected cancer pathway referral for stomach cancer if they: have dysphagia, or are aged 55 and over, with weight loss, and they have any of the following: upper abdominal pain reflux dyspepsia. [2015, amended 2025] 1.2.8 Consider non-urgent , direct access upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to assess for stomach cancer in people with haematemesis. [2015] 1.2.9

[2026] Why the committee made the 2026 recommendations

For the utility of serum CA125 measurement and age thresholds, the committee agreed that using age-based serum CA125 thresholds in women, and trans men and non-binary people with female reproductive organs aged 40 and over can support referral decisions for ultrasound. Moderate-certainty evidence showed that in women over 50, serum CA125 levels meet the predictive value needed to justify a strong recommendation to arrange an ultrasound scan. Based on the clinical and health economic evidence, the committee agreed age-specific thresholds in 10-year age bands for this age group.

For people aged 40 to 49 years, although the evidence was less certain and did not meet the required predictive value needed to justify a strong recommendation to arrange an ultrasound scan, the CA125 threshold of 35 U/ml or over still shows moderate‑to-high sensitivity. The committee agreed that for this age group, the measurement of CA125 remains useful in guiding decisions about further investigations.

The committee acknowledged that the low prevalence of ovarian cancer in younger age groups affects serum CA125 performance, which increases the risk of false reassurance and late diagnosis, particularly in those aged 39 and under. For this age group, the committee agreed that serum CA125 is not sufficiently accurate to support decision making. Therefore, the committee recommended that serum CA125 should not be used in isolation to guide suspected ovarian cancer decisions. The committee recommended considering an ultrasound scan for those with persistent symptoms. The committee also agreed the importance of safety netting for those aged 39 and under, and recommended that if an ultrasound scan is normal, other potential causes of symptoms should be investigated and people advised about when to return to their GP.

The committee agreed that the referral thresholds for serum CA125 should be reflected in the recommendations; they agreed not to label CA125 <35 U/ml as a 'normal' level and emphasised preserving clinical discretion in investigating vague or non-specific symptoms when appropriate. Full details of the evidence and the committee's discussion are in evidence review B: dual testing with serum CA125 and ultrasound scan compared to serum CA125 alone, and age and serum CA125 thresholds for detection of suspected ovarian cancer in adults . How the recommendations might affect practice

Implementing age-based CA125 thresholds may increase the use of ultrasound in people aged 50 and over. The economic analysis suggested that additional annual funding would be needed, mainly because of increased ultrasound and follow-up care. However, as many GPs currently request ultrasound alongside CA125 testing, the recommendations could reduce unnecessary concurrent testing. Introducing age-based CA125 thresholds may also require updates to laboratory reporting systems and clinical pathways.

In the 40 to 49 age group, the current CA125 threshold remains unchanged, so no significant change in practice is expected. For those aged 39 years and under, the recommendations promote clinical judgement and an approach, which may reduce unnecessary CA125 testing but could increase targeted ultrasound use. Given the low prevalence of ovarian cancer in these younger age groups and the high current use of ultrasound in practice, these changes are not expected to have a significant resource impact. There is limited evidence for women, and trans men and non-binary people with female reproductive organs who experience unscheduled vaginal bleeding on sequential or continuous HRT . The British Menopause Society has published guidance on unscheduled bleeding on HRT ( British Menopause Society: Management of unscheduled bleeding on HRT ). [2026] Why the committee made the 2026 recommendations The guideline recommends referral via a suspected cancer pathway for endometrial cancer for people aged 55 and over with post-menopausal bleeding, and consideration of referral for those under 55. These recommendations do not address unscheduled bleeding that may be associated with HRT.

We undertook a systematic review to assess the diagnostic accuracy of unscheduled vaginal bleeding for detecting endometrial cancer in adults taking HRT, to inform referral decisions via a suspected cancer pathway. No relevant studies were identified. In 2024, the British Menopause Society (BMS), in partnership with other specialist organisations and Royal Colleges, published guidance on the 'Management of unscheduled bleeding on hormone replacement therapy (HRT)'. The authors acknowledge a significant lack of evidence in many areas, with recommendations based on expert opinion. The committee noted this and the absence of studies in the NICE systematic review.

The committee discussed the increasing use of HRT (data from the NHS Business Services Authority showed a 47% increase in prescriptions in England in 2022/23) and agreed that recommendations are needed despite the evidence gap. The committee acknowledged that the BMS recommendations are widely used in practice and agreed to signpost to them, while highlighting the lack of evidence and evolving clinical practice. Given the lack of evidence, the committee made a recommendation for research to establish when unscheduled bleeding in those taking HRT should prompt referral via a suspected cancer pathway.

Full details of the evidence and the committee's discussion are in evidence review C: endometrial cancer: unscheduled bleeding, HRT and cancer referral . How the recommendations might affect practice Raising the awareness of the BMS guideline among healthcare professionals could help reduce unnecessary referrals for cases of unscheduled bleeding attributable to HRT. Use clinical judgement Why the committee made the 2021 recommendation

The evidence on the diagnostic accuracy of fixed and age-specific prostate-specific antigen (PSA) thresholds was very uncertain because all of the studies were based on a population that had already been referred to secondary care. The 2019 guideline recommended referral if PSA levels were above the age-specific reference range. The committee agreed that referral should be considered based on PSA thresholds, but did not make a stronger recommendation because of the uncertainty in the evidence and the likely low positive predictive value of the PSA test for prevalence estimates based on UK population data. The committee noted that many prostate cancers are slow growing and might never impact life expectancy. Some might choose not to be referred to secondary care to avoid invasive investigations and treatment that might not benefit them. Therefore, the committee agreed that a patient-centred approach to referral is important, and recommended that personal preferences and any comorbidities should be taken into account.

The committee agreed that more research is needed in this area to better understand the most appropriate thresholds that should prompt referral to secondary care for each age group. The committee noted that ethnicity and family history are important factors that affect the risk of prostate cancer. Therefore, they recommended that the data from research be stratified by these factors to determine whether different PSA levels should prompt referral in these groups. Research in this area may also help to address health inequalities in prostate cancer diagnosis and outcomes in the UK.

There was no strong evidence to differentiate between using age-specific or fixed PSA thresholds. The committee also noted that no cost-effectiveness evidence comparing age-specific thresholds with fixed thresholds was identified. However, because PSA levels increase naturally with age, the committee agreed a lower fixed PSA threshold would detect more cases of prostate cancer but also lead to unnecessary biopsies and overtreatment in some age groups. This would also be likely to result in more referrals to secondary care and have a significant impact on NHS resources. The committee therefore recommended the use of age-specific thresholds, which are already established in current practice and were recommended in the previous version of the guideline. Because of regional variations in practice (particularly in the 50 to 69 age range), the committee decided to define the age-specific PSA thresholds. The committee agreed that the thresholds used in the reviewed studies on people with symptoms of possible prostate cancer should be used in the absence of evidence to support alternative values, because these studies were most applicable to the population that the recommendation applies to. No evidence was available specifically for those under 40 or over 79, and so the committee recommended that clinical judgement is used when deciding whether to refer people in these groups to secondary care.

Full details of the evidence and the committee's discussion are in evidence review A: PSA testing for prostate cancer . How the recommendation might affect practice Referral based on age-specific PSA thresholds is already recommended, so practice should not change significantly. Also, clarifying the age-specific thresholds will help standardise care. Taking into account patient preferences and comorbidities should also lead to a more patient-centred approach to referral. [2015, amended 2026]
Why the committee made the 2026 recommendation

The evidence showed that positive predictive values of 3% or above were seen in people aged 60 and over who presented in primary care with unexplained weight loss (a mean loss of more than 5% of body weight within a 6-month period). Based on this finding, the committee recommended adding age and unexplained weight loss thresholds to the existing recommendation on unexplained weight loss as a non-site-specific symptom of cancer. Although the certainty of the evidence was low – this was a single study without data on sensitivity or specificity to assess imprecision based on the GRADE framework – the study was well-conducted, directly applicable to the UK and based on a sufficiently large sample size. The committee agreed that a potential benefit of this recommendation would be to identify those people with cancer more rapidly highlighting that the use of urgent investigation or a suspected cancer pathway referral or a non-specific symptoms pathway referral should be made. The committee outlined that the choice of referral pathways is related to the person presenting to primary care and clinical judgement. Furthermore, the committee agreed that introducing age thresholds for unexplained weight loss may minimise the number of inappropriate referrals for people without cancer, while maximising the number of appropriate referrals for people with cancer. The committee also agreed to retain the list of potential cancers associated with unexplained weight loss.

The committee acknowledged that the updated recommendation does not apply to adults aged 18 to 59. However, they were reassured that the guideline's recommendations on safety netting allow for reviews of people with any symptom that may be associated with an increased risk of cancer. Full details of the evidence and the committee's discussion are in evidence review D: unexplained weight loss as a non-site specific symptom in adults in primary care) . How the recommendations might affect practice

The committee agreed that the potential benefit of introducing age thresholds for unexplained weight loss could be to save time and resources by reducing the number of unnecessary referrals, while improving the accuracy of referrals for people most at risk of cancer. BACKGROUND & AIMS: Celiac disease is a major public health problem worldwide. Although initially it was reported from countries with predominant Caucasian populations, it now has been reported from other parts of the world. The exact global prevalence of celiac disease is not known. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to estimate the global prevalence of celiac disease.

METHODS: We searched Medline, PubMed, and EMBASE for the keywords celiac disease, celiac, celiac disease, tissue transglutaminase antibody, anti-endomysium antibody, endomysial antibody, and prevalence for studies published from January 1991 through March 2016. Each article was cross-referenced with the words Asia, Europe, Africa, South America, North America, and Australia. The diagnosis of celiac disease was based on European Society of Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Nutrition guidelines. Of 3843 articles, 96 articles were included in the final analysis.

RESULTS: The pooled global prevalence of celiac disease was 1.4% (95% confidence interval, 1.1%-1.7%) in 275,818 individuals, based on positive results from tests for anti-tissue transglutaminase and/or anti-endomysial antibodies (called seroprevalence). The pooled global prevalence of biopsy-confirmed celiac disease was 0.7% (95% confidence interval, 0.5%-0.9%) in 138,792 individuals. The prevalence values for celiac disease were 0.4% in South America, 0.5% in Africa and North America, 0.6% in Asia, and 0.8% in Europe and Oceania; the prevalence was higher in female vs male individuals (0.6% vs 0.4%; P < .001). The prevalence of celiac disease was significantly greater in children than adults (0.9% vs 0.5%; P < .001).

CONCLUSIONS: In a systematic review and meta-analysis, we found celiac disease to be reported worldwide. The prevalence of celiac disease based on serologic test results is 1.4% and based on biopsy results is 0.7%. The prevalence of celiac disease varies with sex, age, and location. There is a need for population-based prevalence studies in many countries. Copyright © 2018 AGA Institute. Published by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved. AIM To critically review the literature addressing the definition, epidemiology, aetiology and pathophysiology of acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (ACPO).

METHODS A systematic search was performed to identify articles investigating the aetiology and pathophysiology of ACPO. A narrative synthesis of the evidence was undertaken. RESULTS No consistent approach to the definition or reporting of ACPO has been developed, which has led to overlapping investigation with other conditions. A vast array of risk factors has been identified, supporting a multifactorial aetiology. The pathophysiological mechanisms remain unclear, but are likely related to altered autonomic regulation of colonic motility, in the setting of other predisposing factors.

CONCLUSION Future research should aim to establish a clear and consistent definition of ACPO, and elucidate the pathophysiological mechanisms leading to altered colonic function. An improved understanding of the aetiology of ACPO may facilitate the development of targeted strategies for its prevention and treatment.

INTRODUCTION Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (ACPO) is a rare condition characterised by acute colonic dilatation in the absence of mechanical obstruction. It was first described by Sir William Ogilvie in 1948, in two patients with malignant infiltration of the pre-vertebral ganglia[ 1 ].

ACPO usually occurs in hospitalised patients with severe illness or trauma, or following general, orthopaedic, neurosurgical, gynaecological or other surgical procedures, with an estimated incidence of 100 cases per 100000 admissions and a mortality rate of 8%[ 2 , 3 ]. Colonic ischaemia or perforation occurs in up to 15%, and is associated with an estimated 40% mortality[ 4 - 6 ]. Therefore, early recognition and appropriate therapy are important determinants of prognosis[ 2 ].

The pathophysiology underlying ACPO is poorly understood, with the prevailing hypothesis being an imbalance in colonic autonomic innervation[ 2 , 4 ]. Progress has been limited by a rudimentary understanding of the complex processes regulating colonic motility patterns, the lack of specific animal models for ACPO, and the poor quality of evidence arising from case reports and uncontrolled case series.

An improved understanding of the mechanisms underlying ACPO may aid the development of novel management strategies for this condition. Therefore, the aim of this systematic review was to critically review the literature addressing the definition, epidemiology, risk factors, aetiology and pathophysiology of ACPO with a view to informing knowledge gaps and identifying priority areas for future research.

MATERIALS AND METHODS A systematic search of the Ovid MEDLINE and Embase databases was performed from inception to 25 May 2017, using the search terms “Ogilvie’s syndrome”, “pseudoobstruction”, and “pseudo obstruction”. Google Scholar was also searched using free text entries. Identified articles were screened by title and abstract for inclusion, with subsequent acquisition of full texts. The reference lists of included papers were manually searched, and a hand search of the scientific literature was performed to identify additional relevant publications.

Non-English articles were excluded. There were no exclusion limits by study design; both primary research and review articles were eligible. Full-text articles were evaluated for evidence addressing the definition, epidemiology, risk factors, aetiology and pathogenesis of ACPO. Clinical management has recently been reviewed in depth[ 7 - 9 ], and was beyond the scope of this study, though pathophysiological hypotheses drawn from this evidence were evaluated. A narrative synthesis of the identified evidence was undertaken.

RESULTS Definitions of ACPO ACPO is characterised by acute colonic dilatation in the absence of intrinsic mechanical obstruction or extrinsic inflammatory process[ 10 ]. ACPO should be distinguished from other acute conditions, such as toxic megacolon, which may have inflammatory or infective causes, as well as chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction (CIPO) and other causes of megacolon.

Many overlapping terms have been used in the literature to describe ACPO since its original description, reflecting the uncertainly regarding its precise aetiology (Table 1 ). The term “intestinal pseudo-obstruction” was first proposed by Dudley in 1958[ 11 ], with “ACPO” not appearing for another twenty years[ 4 ]. Use of “Ogilvie’s syndrome” has been discouraged due to ambiguity regarding its meaning[ 12 ], though considerable heterogeneity in terminology still exists in recent literature[ 3 , 13 , 14 ]. Inconsistent terminology has contributed to inconsistency in research and reporting. No standardised clinical definition or diagnostic criteria for ACPO were identified[ 15 ], preventing reliable synthesis of data on risk factors or therapeutic strategies[ 7 , 8 ]. Some studies failed to distinguish ACPO from CIPO and other forms of megacolon[ 10 , 16 ], despite these being distinct entities with different mechanisms and therapies[ 17 , 18 ].

Epidemiology ACPO is uncommon, with an identified incidence of approximately 100 cases per 100000 inpatient admissions[ 3 ]. A recent US study reported a declining mortality rate associated with ACPO from 9.4% in 1998 to 6.4% in 2011, although over-diagnosis may have contributed[ 3 ]; historically mortality rates were as high as 30%[ 4 ]. Colonic perforation and ischemia occur in 10%-20%, with an associated mortality of up to 45%[ 2 , 4 ]. Rates of surgical and endoscopic intervention have declined in recent decades, due to an increasing focus on conservative management and pharmacological therapy with neostigmine[ 3 ].

ACPO disproportionately affects elderly and comorbid patients; often those with an acute illness on a background of chronic cardiac, respiratory or neurological disease. ACPO also occurs following general, orthopaedic, neurosurgical, cardiothoracic and gynaecological procedures[ 19 ]. Vanek et al[ 2 ] reported 400 cases of ACPO, with approximately 50% resulting from acute medical illness and 50% from post-surgical patients. Incidence rates have been described in spinal or orthopaedic surgery (1%-2%)[ 13 , 20 ], cardiac bypass (up to 5%)[ 21 ], and following burn injuries (0.3%)[ 22 ]. An abundance of other conditions associated with ACPO were found to have been reported in the literature, the most common of which are summarised (Table 2 ).

Pathophysiology Review of the literature revealed a vast array of risk factors for ACPO, supporting a multifactorial aetiology with several pathways leading to a common effect on colonic motor function[ 23 ] (Figure 1 ). However, few published studies were found directly investigating the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying ACPO, with the majority of evidence inferred from basic physiology and other disease states such as post-operative ileus (POI). No animal models of ACPO were identified. Figure 1 Pathophysiological factors that have been implicated in the development of acute colonic pseudo-obstruction.
